messages.help.issues.title: About this section
messages.help.issues.body: Issues are events automatically grouped by similar errors: the same exception type and code location are merged into one issue with a stack trace, frequency, and occurrence history.
messages.help.performance.title: About this section
messages.help.performance.body: This page lists your application's transactions and endpoints with response-time percentiles (p50/p95/p99), error rate, and Apdex — useful for spotting the slowest and least stable spots.
messages.help.metrics.title: About this section
messages.help.metrics.body: Metrics are time series of arbitrary numeric application values (counters, histograms) that can be aggregated and viewed over a chosen time period.
messages.help.uptime.title: About this section
messages.help.uptime.body: Monitors periodically check the availability of your services and create incidents on failures — this page shows current status, incident history, and uptime percentage.
messages.help.alerts.title: About this section
messages.help.alerts.body: Alert rules define which events (new issue, regression, error spike) trigger notifications, and channels define where they are delivered (email and other integrations).
messages.help.alertdeliveries.title: About this section
messages.help.alertdeliveries.body: This page shows the most recent failed deliveries of notifications to channels (email, webhook, Telegram) — with the error text and the number of attempts.
messages.help.maintenance.title: About this section
messages.help.maintenance.body: Maintenance windows let you temporarily pause monitor checks so planned work doesn't create false incidents and notifications — one-off or weekly, by weekday and time.
messages.help.statuspages.title: About this section
messages.help.statuspages.body: A public status page shows visitors the current state of selected monitors without giving them access to the rest of the project — a convenient way to keep users informed during an incident.
messages.help.probes.title: About this section
messages.help.probes.body: Probes are agents in different regions that run monitor checks from that location — this lets you confirm a service is reachable from more than one place and tell a service outage apart from a region-specific network problem.
messages.help.metricalerts.title: About this section
messages.help.metricalerts.body: Metric alert rules watch a chosen metric (an aggregation compared against a threshold over a time window) and open an incident when the condition is met — this page also shows the history of past incidents.
messages.help.webvitals.title: About this section
messages.help.webvitals.body: Web Vitals are real-user page load experience metrics: LCP (main content render speed), INP (responsiveness to interaction), and CLS (visual stability). The good / needs-improvement / poor thresholds are Google's standard Web Vitals bounds, the same for everyone and not configurable per project.
messages.help.profiles.title: About this section
messages.help.profiles.body: Profiles show where CPU time goes inside your code: expand a group of profiles for the selected period into a flame graph to see the "heaviest" functions by self-CPU share.
messages.help.perfissues.title: About this section
messages.help.perfissues.body: Automatically detected performance problems: N+1 database queries, slow queries, and HTTP floods, each with the code location and how often it occurs.
messages.help.regressions.title: About this section
messages.help.regressions.body: Regressions are a sustained worsening of an endpoint's p95 duration or a web vital's p75 compared to a recent baseline: baseline, peak, and percent increase are shown so you can quickly gauge the severity.
messages.help.profileregressions.title: About this section
messages.help.profileregressions.body: Profile regressions track a function's self-CPU share growing over time — a way to spot code that used to be cheap becoming noticeably slower, before users complain.
messages.brand.tagline: Catch errors before your users do.

messages.perf.help.events: Number of transactions (samples) recorded for this endpoint over the selected window.
messages.perf.help.throughput: Request rate — the average number of transactions per unit of time over the window.
messages.perf.help.p50: Median latency: half of the requests are faster than this value.
messages.perf.help.p75: 75th percentile: three quarters of the requests are faster than this value.
messages.perf.help.p95: 95th percentile: 95% of requests are faster; the slow tail begins here. A good SLO target.
messages.perf.help.p99: 99th percentile: the slowest 1% of requests — shows the impact of the worst cases.
messages.perf.help.failure: Share of transactions with an error status among all transactions in the window.
messages.perf.help.apdex: Apdex — user-satisfaction score from 0 to 1 against a threshold T: requests up to T count as satisfied, up to 4×T as tolerating, slower as frustrated. 1 = all fast, 0 = all slow.
messages.perf.help.p95_period: p95 latency over time for the window — the trend of the slow tail, not a single number.
messages.perf.vital.help.lcp: Largest Contentful Paint — time until the largest element on screen finishes rendering; how quickly the main content becomes visible.
messages.perf.vital.help.inp: Interaction to Next Paint — delay between a user action (click, tap, keypress) and the screen updating; overall responsiveness.
messages.perf.vital.help.cls: Cumulative Layout Shift — how much the page jumps around while loading; visual stability. Lower is better.
messages.perf.vital.help.fcp: First Contentful Paint — time until the first piece of content (text or image) appears on screen.
messages.perf.vital.help.ttfb: Time to First Byte — time until the server sends the first byte of the response; backend and network latency.

messages.perf.kind.explain.n_plus_one: The same query runs many times in a loop — one row at a time instead of one batched fetch. Usually an ORM loading related records one by one.
messages.perf.kind.fix.n_plus_one: Load the related data at once: eager-loading, a JOIN, or a single query with IN (...).
messages.perf.kind.explain.slow_db_query: A single query runs longer than the threshold and takes a noticeable share of the response time.
messages.perf.kind.fix.slow_db_query: Check the plan (EXPLAIN) and indexes on the WHERE/JOIN columns; avoid SELECT * and unindexed sorts, and narrow the rows scanned.
messages.perf.kind.explain.http_flood: One request makes many sequential outbound HTTP calls — they run one after another and add up into the latency.
messages.perf.kind.fix.http_flood: Run the calls in parallel, or replace them with a single batched request to the upstream service.
messages.perf.kind.explain.default: This transaction spends an outsized amount of time in one repeated or slow operation.
messages.perf.kind.fix.default: Open the sample trace to see which span dominates the time, and reduce or batch it.

messages.project.settings.perf.sample_rate.help: Share of transactions kept for performance analysis (1 = all, 0.1 = one in ten). Lower saves storage but makes the stats coarser.
messages.project.settings.perf.apdex_ms.help: Response time (ms) considered 'satisfying' for the Apdex score. Faster counts as satisfied, up to 4× as tolerable, slower as frustrating.
messages.project.settings.perf.n_plus_one_min.hel: How many repeated similar queries in a row count as an N+1 problem (many near-identical queries instead of one batched call).
messages.project.settings.perf.n_plus_one_total_m: Minimum combined time (ms) of a repeated-query series before it is flagged as N+1. Filters out small, harmless series.
messages.project.settings.perf.slow_db_ms.help: Threshold (ms) above which a single database query is considered slow and raised as a performance issue.
messages.project.settings.perf.http_flood_min.hel: How many outbound HTTP calls in one transaction count as a 'flood' — a sign of excessive calls to external services.
messages.project.settings.regressions.threshold_p: How many percent a metric must rise above its rolling baseline to declare a regression (e.g. 25 = a quarter slower).
messages.project.settings.regressions.recovery_pc: How far the metric must return toward the baseline to close the regression. Hysteresis — prevents flapping open/closed at the edge.
messages.project.settings.regressions.window_minu: Window (minutes) over which the current metric value is computed for comparison against the baseline.
messages.project.settings.regressions.min_samples: Minimum number of samples in the window before a regression is evaluated — guards against false alarms on sparse data.
messages.project.settings.regressions.duration_fl: Minimum duration (ms) below which growth is ignored: 2 ms → 4 ms is +100% but not a real problem.
messages.project.settings.regressions.floor_lcp.h: Floor for LCP (ms): LCP regressions below this absolute value are not raised (too small to matter).
messages.project.settings.regressions.floor_inp.h: Floor for INP (ms): INP regressions below this absolute value are not raised.
messages.project.settings.regressions.floor_cls.h: Floor for CLS (unitless): CLS regressions below this absolute value are not raised.
messages.project.settings.regressions.floor_fcp.h: Floor for FCP (ms): FCP regressions below this absolute value are not raised.
Floor for TTFB (ms): TTFB regressions below this absolute value are not raised.

messages.help.incidents.title: What is this section?
messages.help.incidents.body: An incident opens when a monitor fails the configured number of times in a row and closes when it answers again. This page shows what broke, when, for how long — and whether it fell inside a maintenance window.
messages.help.cardinality.title: What is this section?
messages.help.cardinality.body: Cardinality is the number of distinct values a field takes: transaction name, environment, metric name. An identifier that ends up in a name (/users/42 instead of /users/{id}) turns one name into millions and makes charts useless. This page shows which fields hit the ceiling and which values were collapsed.
messages.help.teams.title: What is this section?
messages.help.teams.body: A team is a named group of organization members. Teams grant no permissions on their own: they exist so alerts can address a group instead of listing people by name in every channel.
